headline: New moon springs load up The Race as PM flood window fires for big bass
subhead: Bigger tides, faster current, and a sunset high stand that lines up perfect — here's where the eastern Sound is producing and where it's still a grind.
body_markdown:
Last week the eastern Sound was still settling out from the blow that rolled through around the holiday. Current at The Race and Plum Gut was running hard and dirty for two days after, and honestly the bite was inconsistent — you had to time it right or you were fishing chop and foam for nothing. Water temps have been climbing across the western basin, and that heat is starting to push east. It's not blown out at Fishers Island or Orient yet, but the signal is there — bait's getting nervous, and fish are repositioning off the structure they've held on for weeks.

This week changes the math. We're building into new moon springs, with peak tidal range hitting Saturday through Monday, July 11–13. That's the number that matters. Bigger tides mean more water moving through Plum Gut and The Race in less time — current speeds that were pushing 3-4 knots on a normal cycle are going to spike closer to 5, maybe more on the max ebb through the Gut. The piece that's got me setting my week around it: the evening high stand is converging with sunset right through this window. That's the PM flood-sunset striper setup I wait all year for — moving water and low light stacking on top of each other at the exact same hours the big fish want to feed. First real shot at that alignment since the June full moon, and it's not subtle when it lines up.

Stripers have been scattered but not absent. I've had two solid nights out of three on the west side of Plum Gut, working the eddy line where the outgoing current wraps around the can off Orient Point Light. Eels on a fish-finder rig, dead-drifted right along the seam where fast water meets the slower back-eddy — that's been the money presentation on the last two hours of the ebb. Bigger fish, 30 to low-40s, are holding deeper than you'd think, 25 to 35 feet, sitting in the slack behind the boulders rather than up in the current lane itself. Surface plugs — Gibbs pencils, big Danny-style swimmers — have worked the last 45 minutes of light at The Race, but you need to be working structure, not open rip. The fish aren't chasing bait into the teeth of 4 knots of current; they're ambushing it where the current breaks.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player right now. Fishers Island's west end and the rips off Race Rock have had real blitzes on peanut bunker pushed through by the tide — 8 to 12 pound blues tearing up bait on top during the first two hours of the outgoing. Bucktails with a strip of pork rind, or just a diamond jig ripped fast through the melee, will get bit instantly. If you see the surface nervous with bunker balling up tight, don't wait — that window closes fast once the current slacks.

Fluke has been a mixed bag, and I want to be straight about it. The bay-side bite around Mattituck and Southold has gone quiet as water temps up there pushed into the high 70s — too warm, fish don't want it. What's happening instead is a shift out toward the inlets and the open Sound, where upwelled water is running cooler, close to 71 degrees, and holding way more life. I've been picking at keeper fluke — nothing giant, mostly 18 to 22 inches with a few better ones mixed in — drifting the mouth of Plum Gut on the last of the incoming, using 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, bounced slow along bottom in 30 to 40 feet. It's not a bang-bang bite. You've got to cover water and stay patient through the drift, but the fish that are there are quality.

Porgies have been a dependable backup when the bigger stuff isn't cooperating — Fishers Island rockpiles and the humps off Plum Gut are stacked with them, sandworms or clam on a simple high-low rig in 20 to 30 feet, any stage of tide that isn't dead slack. Good for keeping a rod bent while you wait out a slow stretch on stripers.

Weakfish, I've got nothing to report, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Water's been warm enough for weeks now and there's been zero sign of them showing in this zone. That temperature threshold everyone points to isn't the trigger people thought it was — something else has to click, and right now it hasn't.

One more thing worth watching heading into next week: there's early bonito and false albacore chatter building from Block Island east, and that warm-water corridor is spreading toward Fishers Island rather than staying pinned to Block. I haven't seen fish yet off Orient or the Race, but if that pattern holds, don't be shocked if the first schoolie albies show up working the rips off Fishers by the end of the month. I'll be watching the outer edge of the Race for diving birds on my way out to the striper grounds — that's usually the first tip.

My plan for the week: hit the Saturday and Sunday sunset flood at Plum Gut and The Race while the tide-light window is locked in, eels first, pencils as backup when the light gets low enough. If the bass don't show, I'm sliding to the fluke drift off the Gut on the last two hours of incoming — cooler water, active fish, and a decent floor under a slow night. Either way, with tides this big, something's going to be moving through that current.
